summary.value: This paper proposes TS-REASONER, a two-stage framework that aligns a Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) with an LLM for time-series understanding and reasoning. The authors evaluate on TimeSeriesExam and MTBench, reporting gains over same-size LLM/VLM/TS-LLM baselines.

strengths.value:
The two-stage design (alignment → instruction tuning) is easy to follow.

Shows improvements on both benchmarks against same-size LLM/VLM/TS-LLM.

 Removing Stage-1/Stage-2, attributes/LLM-caption, or the TSFM all lead to notable drops.

Implementation is provided.

weaknesses.value:
Undefined “time-series reasoning.” The paper does not clearly define the term. The main benchmark, TimeSeriesExam, is positioned as a time-series understanding exam and mainly tests recognition/comprehension.

Limited novelty. The pipeline—TSFM representations → adapter to LLM embeddings → two stages (caption-alignment pretrain → instruction tuning)—is very close to prior work (e.g., ChatTS with attribute-aware synthetic series + textual descriptions + alignment training; ChatTime on unified time-series↔text modeling).

Narrow evaluation. Focuses on template multiple-choice tasks; lacks open-ended QA and natural-language explanations (e.g., the open-QA setup used in ChatTS).

Inconsistent trainable modules. The main text states “TSFM frozen, LLM trainable,” while the appendix says “all backbone parameters are finetuned.” This conflict affects reproducibility and cost claims.

Insufficient statistical robustness. Missing multi-seed results, confidence intervals, or bootstrap tests; some gains appear within typical variance.

Efficiency claims lack evidence. No end-to-end measurements for training time, peak memory, inference latency/throughput, or cost per accuracy/token, which are needed to support the efficiency claim.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors proposed a new way to align time series foundation models with LLM to enhance its reasoning ability. Specifically, the authors used the embedding of a frozen TSFM as input and map the embedding to the semantic space of text input. They further proposed a captioning method to generate the training data. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model TS-REASONER.

strengths.value:
S1: The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
S2: The idea of integrating TSFM with LLM is interesting and sounds technical.
S3: Extensive experiments are conducted.

weaknesses.value:
W1: There are two factors affects the results (the third one two-stage training is from existing work): 1). Use TSFM's embedding as input. 2). Generated a caption dataset for alignment. It is not clear which one contributes to the final improvement. I would suggest doing the following control experiments: a) training ChatTS with the generated datasets to see whether using generated datasets can improve performance. b) training TS-Reasoner with ChatTS's datasets to show whether using TSFM can improve performance.
W2: The authors did not mention whether they would share the trained model and the generated caption datasets, which would make the reproducibility of the paper a bit difficult.

questions.value:
Q1: Did the authors evaluate the reasoning model (e.g. deepseek-R1)? They are expected to perform better on reasoning tasks.
Q2: I am not sure whether the proposed approach has a data leakage risk. Are there any overlaps between the time series datasets used to train TimesFM and those in TimeSeriesExam and MTBench?

**General Response**

We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and the time spent evaluating our work. We are encouraged that reviewers recognized the novelty of our problem formulation (P6KN) and the strong performance (cNdi), and found the paper well-written (Fudn, cNdi, P6KN). Below, we address the specific concerns regarding our contributions.

Contributions:

- **Novel Problem**: We introduce the alignment problem between Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) and LLMs. This problem is fundamental to building more solid time series reasoning models by efficiently leveraging the pretrained knowledge of both TSFMs and LLMs, opening up more routes for future models.
- **Technical Contributions (I)**: Unlike recent works [1, 2] that train time series encoders from scratch or require heavy finetuning, our TSFM-LLM alignment paradigm preserves pretrained temporal representations. This design leads to superior performance with substantially improved data efficiency, enabling us to outperform baselines while saving more than 50% of training data.

- **Technical Contributions (II)**: ChatTS [1] relies on templates to synthesize captions, and [2] adopts the vanilla instructions by humans. In contrast, we propose Attribute-Aware Captioning, which enriches the timeseries-text pairs with greater details and higher linguistic diversity. It improves alignment quality and reasoning performance, as validated in Section 4.5 and Appendix C.

- **Empirical Contributions**: We conduct extensive experiments and compare with 13 models, demonstrating our approach induced substantial improvements on various time series reasoning tasks.

References:

[1] Xie, Zhe, Zeyan Li, Xiao He, Longlong Xu, Xidao Wen, Tieying Zhang, Jianjun Chen, Rui Shi, and Dan Pei. "Chatts: Aligning time series with llms via synthetic data for enhanced understanding and reasoning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.03104 (2024).

[2] Chow, W., Gardiner, L., Hallgrímsson, H. T., Xu, M. A., & Ren, S. Y. (2024). Towards time series reasoning with llms. arXiv preprint arXiv:2409.11376.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for your careful reading and valuable feedback on our paper. Below, we provide detailed responses to the weaknesses raised in your review.

__Q1__: Definition of "Time series reasoning". 

__A1__: We sincerely appreciate your question. **Time series reasoning** leverages LLM's prior knowledge to analyze input time series and performs sophisticated reasoning for generating a textual answer. It differs from time series forecasting and prediction tasks due to the dependency on language capabilities and prior knowledge. 

Given a natural language context $\mathcal{x}$, which may encode background domain knowledge or prompt instructions, and a corresponding set of time series $\mathcal{S} = \lbrace \mathcal{T}_0, \mathcal{T}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{T}_K \rbrace$
, the model $\mathcal{M}$ produces an output sequence $\mathcal{y}$ that may include:

- tokens providing intermediate explanations or descriptions for problem-solving 
- tokens for the final answer or conclusion

The model defines a probability distribution over the output sequence $y$, conditioned on inputs $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{x}$. Specifically, 

$$
P_M(y \mid x, \mathcal{S}) = \sum_{r} P(y|r,x, S)P(r|x, S)
$$

where $r$ represents the reasoning path that explains why it leads to the answer, we will add the definition in the main text.

__Q2__: Difference from ChatTS [1] and ChatTime [2]

__A2__: Thank you for your question. We clarify the differences as follows:

(I) **Difference from ChatTS (fewer but higher-quality synthetic data + frozen TSFM)**: We developed a novel attribute-aware captioning method to generate more diverse and higher-quality captions for TSFM-LLM alignment; we leveraged a pretrained TSFM and froze it during training, while ChatTS needs to train a time series encoder from scratch, which requires massive time series-text pairing data. Due to these differences, our TS-Reasoner outperforms ChatTS with 50% less training data. 

(II) **Difference from ChatTime (leveraging a pretrained TSFM to save training cost and data)**: ChatTime needs to train LLMs for language modeling of time series and understanding their numerical tokens, which requires 1 million pre-training samples. In contrast, TS-Reasoner avoids this costly learning stage and generation of numerical tokens. It only needs to focus on TSFM-LLM alignment between a pretrained TSFM and an LLM. This shifts the burden from Translation to pure Reasoning, yielding greater efficiency and deeper semantic understanding.

__Q3__: Evaluation on Open-ended time series reasoning problems.

__A3__: Thank you for your suggestion. We followed your suggestion to evaluate on the inductive reasoning dataset from ChatTS [1] and evaluate  RAGAS[]. TS-Reasoner outperforms ChatTS and demonstrates superior capability in solving open-ended time series reasoning problems.

|TS-Reasoner|54.7|

__A4__: Thank you for raising this important problem! We froze the TSFM backbone to preserve its pretrained priors. Only the projector and the LLM are trainable. We will revise Line 740 to make it clearer.

__Q5__: Insufficient statistical robustness and variance.

__A5__: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We follow your suggestions to conduct 3 independent runs with temperature 0.7, the results (Mean $\pm$ Std. Dev.) below demonstrate that our method yields consistent and stable performance over baselines:

Thank you for the comments! We note that most concerns focus on the comparison between our TS-Reasoner and [1]. We would like to point out their fundamental differences in several aspects. 

__Q1__: Novelty and Difference from [1] (Chow et al.)

__A1__: Thank you for this question. We would like to clarify that our method does **not** "copy how [1] generates synthetic time-series." (quoted from reviewer comments). Unlike [1], TS-Reasoner does **not** generate synthetic time series. This is a fundamental difference in our proposed paradigm:

**Novel Problem**:
- We introduce the alignment problem between Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) and LLMs. This problem is fundamental to building more solid time series reasoning models by efficiently leveraging the pretrained knowledge of both TSFMs and LLMs, opening up more routes for future models.

**Technical Contributions (I)**: 
- Our TSFM-LLM alignment paradigm preserves pretrained temporal representations, unlike [1], which trains time series encoders from scratch. This design leads to superior performance with substantially improved data efficiency, enabling us to outperform baselines while saving more than 50% of training data.

**Technical Contributions (II)**:
- TS-Reasoner (Ours) synthesizes timeseries-text paris on off-the-shelf synthetic and real-world time series. We do not use attributes to generate new time series. Instead, we utilize them to distill knowledge from the pre-trained Foundation Models (e.g., GPT-4.1). Our goal is to align the temporal knowledge of a pretrained TSFM with LLM reasoning. [1] relies on a generator to create synthetic, rule-based time series (e.g., sine waves, linear trends) and leverage vanilla instruction prompts to generated captions. This approach is validated inferior compared to our proposed attribute-aware captionging in Section 4.5.

We will add the above discussion of [1] in the main paper.

__Q2__: The significance of Attribute-Aware Captioning.

__A2__: Thanks for your question. Our attribute-aware captioning fundamentally differs from the simple caption instruction used in [1].

- **Qualitative Difference**: As detailed in Table 5 and Appendix C, rigid templates (e.g., "The trend is upward") used by [1] struggle to convey the subtle numerical dynamics required for complex deduction. In contrast, our method produces dense, context-rich captions.
- **Quantitative Impact**: Our ablation study (Section 4.5) demonstrates that our captions' linguistic diversity is essential. Removing attribute-awareness results in a significant performance drop, confirming that rich semantic bridges are a prerequisite for effectively interpreting embedding produced by pretrained TSFMs.

__Q3__: K-indicator for multiple time series when the paper provides no experiments or discussion demonstrating its usefulness.

__A3__: Our experiments on Timeseriesexam demonstrate the effectiveness of K-indicator, as 31.8% instances in Timeseriesexam contain 2 time series. The K-indicator acts as a separator between time series in the embedding space, and indicates the position of the $k$-th time series. The results of the Timeseriesexam indicate the effectiveness of TS-Reasoner on handling multiple time series, and it is compatible with more time series scenarios.

References:

[1] Chow, Winnie, et al. "Towards time series reasoning with llms." arXiv preprint arXiv:2409.11376 (2024).

summary.value:
This paper proposes TS-REASONER, a framework designed to enhance time series reasoning by aligning a pre-trained Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) with a Large Language Model (LLM). Its core architecture consists of a frozen, pre-trained TSFM (TimesFM) for encoding time series patches , a trainable TS-to-Text adapter (MLP) to project these features , and a pre-trained LLM (Qwen-2.5-7B).
The model employs a two-stage training process: (1) an alignment pre-training stage, and (2) an instruction fine-tuning stage.
A key contribution is the "attribute-aware captioning" method developed to address the scarcity of time series-text pairs. This method involves generating high-quality, diverse captions by feeding an advanced VLM (like GPT-4.1) visual plots of the time series, along with prompts enriched with key attributes (e.g., trend, periodicity, noise).
Extensive experiments on the TimeSeriesExam and MTBench benchmarks demonstrate that TS-REASONER significantly outperforms LLM, VLM, and TSLLM baselines of comparable size and shows remarkable data efficiency.

strengths.value:
• Novel Data Curation Method: The "attribute-aware captioning" method is the core strength. Using a VLM to process time series plots (rather than raw numerical strings) to generate rich, diverse captions creatively solves a well-known data scarcity problem in the field.

• Strong Empirical Performance: The paper demonstrates SOTA results, with TS-REASONER significantly outperforming a wide range of similarly-sized baselines (LLMs, VLMs, TSLLMs) on two challenging benchmarks.

• Data and Parameter Efficiency: The framework is highly efficient. By leveraging a pre-trained and frozen TSFM, the model inherits a strong foundation for temporal understanding, allowing it to achieve superior performance with less than half the training data of baselines like ChatTS-7B. This makes the approach highly practical.

• Thorough Ablation and Analysis: The paper includes comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3) that validate every key design choice: the necessity of the TSFM, the importance of the attribute-aware captions, and the contribution of each training stage. Further analysis on TSFM (Table 2) and LLM (Figure 6) choices also supports the claims.

• Clarity: The paper's writing and organization are excellent. Figures 3 and 4 are clear, intuitive visualizations of the model architecture and the novel captioning workflow.

weaknesses.value:
• Reliance on Proprietary Models: The key contribution (attribute-aware captioning) relies on an advanced proprietary model, GPT-4.1, to generate the training data. While the paper shows this is effective (Figure 7 demonstrates GPT-4.1 captions work best ), this creates a dependency and a potential reproducibility challenge, as the alignment data quality is tied to the capability of an external, closed-source model.

• Limited Exploration of TSFMs: The paper primarily uses TimesFM. While Table 2 compares it to MOMENT, the paper would be stronger if it explored a wider range of modern TSFMs (e.g., Chronos, Moirai) as the backbone. This would help establish the generality of the "frozen TSFM" approach.

• Insufficient Justification for "Frozen" TSFM: The TSFM is kept frozen throughout training. The ablation in Table 3 ("-TSFM") removes it entirely, which is a different experiment. A more direct ablation would compare a frozen TSFM to a fine-tuned TSFM. While fine-tuning might risk catastrophic forgetting, it could also potentially improve alignment. The paper's justification of "preserv[ing] its pretrained temporal knowledge" is intuitive but not empirically compared against the fine-tuning alternative.

questions.value:
• Keeping the TSFM parameters frozen is a key design choice. The ablation in Table 3 compares this to removing the TSFM. Did the authors experiment with fine-tuning the TSFM (i.e., not freezing it) during the alignment or instruction-tuning stages? If so, how did its performance and training stability compare to the frozen approach?

• The data efficiency results in Figure 5 are impressive. The comparison is made to ChatTS-7B, which the authors note trains its time series encoder from scratch. Is the efficiency gain primarily due to using a pre-trained TSFM, rather than the novel captioning method? How data-efficient is TS-REASONER if trained only on the template data from (Xie et al., 2024), without the new LLM-generated captions? This would help isolate the efficiency contribution of the captioning method itself.

• The captioning process relies heavily on plotting the time series as an image and using a VLM. The qualitative case study in Figure 9 suggests this is superior to using raw text. Was a quantitative comparison performed? For example, what is the performance of TS-REASONER if trained on captions generated by GPT-4.1 (a strong LLM) using the numerical string (not the plot) as input? This would further validate the importance of the visual representation for caption generation.

summary.value: This paper introduces TS-REASONER, a framework designed to improve the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models for time series analysis. The core idea is to align the representations of a specialized Time Series Foundation Model with the input of an LLM, combining the TSFM's strength in capturing temporal patterns with the LLM's advanced reasoning skills in a 2 stage approach of first learning time-series alignment, then finetuning via instruction tuning.

strengths.value:
* Wide range of baselines in evaluation and good exploration of scaling. 
* Code release at submission time

weaknesses.value:
* My primary concern is that this paper seems to be over-claiming on their novelty by stating "our work makes unique contributions .... sets up connection between the connection between TSFMs and LLMS .... simple yet effective time series caption method...". From what I understand of this paper, most of it seems very similar if not exactly the same as the prior work [1]. The 2 stage approach with alignment + fine-tuning, exactly mimics the approach used in [1]. For example, the "G pertinent attributes of time-series" in stage 1, directly copies how [1] generates synthetic time-series and captions. Additionally, in the Ablation studies, "(1) Attribute-aware captioning is critical for robust language-timeseries alignment" and "(2) Absence of any training stage significantly harms the performance. " were key insights already found in [1]. There is no discussion in this paper about the parallels of this work to [1] as well, which makes this all the more concerning. 
* I acknowledge that there are minor changes from [1], but such changes are incremental i.e. using an LLM prompt to help generate synthetic text instead of template only. I define these as incremental because there is not an in depth analysis on how the prompting improves diversity compared to a template.
* Another similarity to [1] is the ts-to-text adapter, but a K indicator is used for multiple time-series as input. However, I can't seem to find any results or discussion of the actual datasets or experimental results that exploit this property, either via multivariate time-series or using multiple at once. 
* Further experimental results explore unnecessary directions, such as differing TSFMs or differing LLMs. This is unnecessary because the methodology does not depend on the pre-trained methodology, so any results do not yield further insight other than "this pre-trained model did better for some abstract reason".

[1] Chow, Winnie, et al. "Towards time series reasoning with llms." arXiv preprint arXiv:2409.11376 (2024).
